source_metadata.title: A Retrospective Observational Study of Adverse Reactions Associated With Intravenous Immunoglobulin Infusion

extraction_metadata.scope_note: Primary-study methods, population, IVIG exposure, adverse-reaction definitions, key incidence estimates, multivariable risk estimates, adverse-event phenotypes, stated limitation, conclusions, data availability, ethics, and conflict disclosure were atomized. Bibliographic entries were not atomized. The low-dose patient-count inconsistency between prose and Table 3 is preserved in SEA rather than converted into a reconciled quantitative atom.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study investigated patient and treatment characteristics associated with immediate adverse reactions during IVIG infusion.
Investigators conducted a single-hospital retrospective chart review at Aichi Medical University covering all patients who received IVIG from 1 May 2014 through 31 December 2018.

The study population comprised patients who received IVIG during the study period for recognized indications in Japan, including immunodeficiency, sepsis, Kawasaki disease, ITP, neuromuscular, dermatologic, and other autoimmune conditions.

population.label: All IVIG recipients at Aichi Medical University from 2014-05-01 through 2018-12-31
inclusion_criteria: Received IVIG during the study period

atoms.canonical_statement: IVIG was administered according to manufacturer infusion protocols, starting at about 0.01 mL/kg/min and increasing over 1 hour to a prescribed maximum below 0.06 mL/kg/min.

exposures.details: Started about 0.01 mL/kg/min; increased over 1 hour; maximum prescribed rate <0.06 mL/kg/min

atoms.canonical_statement: Data were aggregated from physician and nurse notes, prescriptions, medication administration records, and other medical-record documents using a uniform collection sheet.
An immediate infusion-related adverse reaction was defined as a reaction occurring during IVIG infusion and diagnosed by a physician.

outcome.definition: Reaction during an IVIG infusion diagnosed by a physician.

atoms.canonical_statement: Mild reactions caused minimal discomfort and required neither treatment nor infusion interruption; moderate reactions caused intolerable moderate discomfort and required interruption; severe reactions interrupted infusion, produced sequelae, and required prolonged treatment.

outcome.definition: Mild, moderate, or severe according to treatment/interruption, discomfort, sequelae, and prolonged treatment requirements.

atoms.canonical_statement: Descriptive comparisons used chi-square tests for categorical variables and Wilcoxon tests for continuous variables; logistic regression estimated odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals for adverse-reaction risk factors with a significance threshold of 0.05.
Risk-factor regression focused on the higher-incidence subgroup of patients aged at least 15 years with autoimmune disease and evaluated sex, age, neuromuscular diagnosis, and IVIG dose categories.
The cohort included 748 patients: 389 male and 359 female, with mean age 41.7 years and range 0 to 99 years.

population.label: All IVIG recipients

atoms.canonical_statement: Among 748 patients, 377 had autoimmune diseases, including 71 with neuromuscular disease, 58 with dermatologic disease, 61 with ITP, 16 with EGPA, and 171 with Kawasaki disease; 64 had hypogammaglobulinemia and 296 had sepsis.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study observed 4,070 IVIG infusions, including 2,856 for autoimmune disease, 288 for hypogammaglobulinemia, 904 for sepsis, and 22 for other conditions.

atoms.canonical_statement: Average cumulative IVIG dose per patient body weight was 3.7 g/kg for autoimmune disease, compared with 0.6 g/kg for hypogammaglobulinemia and 0.4 g/kg for sepsis.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that female sex, neuromuscular disease, and higher cumulative IVIG dose per body weight were significant patient-level risk factors for adverse reactions.
At the infusion level, the authors identified female sex, age below 60 years, and neuromuscular disease as significant risk factors, whereas dose per infusion did not emerge as a risk factor.
The authors explicitly identified the retrospective nature of the analysis as a study limitation.

The authors stated that neuromuscular disease emerged as a factor contributing to IVIG-associated adverse reactions and that more detailed individual-patient analyses may support future safety recommendations.
The article states that original study contributions are included in the article or supplementary material and that further inquiries may be directed to the corresponding author.
The study was approved by Aichi Medical University (Approval No. 2021-043), and participants provided written informed consent.
The authors declared that the research was conducted without commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
